registers.role: treatment / controls / sample frame: monthly employee-level occupation, total pay and total hours worked for all employees working in Denmark
variables_mentioned: total hours worked in the month
earnings including non-wage benefits (retirement contributions, free residence, phone, PC, bonus, severance)

registers.role: controls / linkage: annual worker demographics, hours based on November status and retirement contributions
variables_mentioned: experience (sum of hours worked in the labor market)

registers.role: outcomes / sample frame: firm accounts (revenue, cost of intermediate inputs, capital, investment), the basis for national accounts
variables_mentioned: value added (revenue less the cost of intermediate inputs)

registers.name_in_paper: American Community Survey (ACS), via Goldin (2014) and Erosa et al. (2022)
registers.role: comparison sample (US pay gap in Table 1) and occupation hours measure
variables_mentioned: log of average hours worked in the occupation

registers.role: occupation characteristics: standardized flexibility index (time pressure, interpersonal relationships, contact with others, structured versus unstructured work, freedom to make decisions)

linkages: eIncome employee records linked to firm value added in FIRE via the firm identifier
Worker demographic information (children's birthdates, marriage, education, age, experience) added from IDA to the income registers merged with FIRE
Motherhood defined from the birthdate of all children recorded in IDA
O*Net/ACS occupation measures matched to Danish 3-digit ISCO occupation codes following Humlum and Meyer (2020)

sample.universe: Employees working in Denmark and the private-sector firms that employ them, as recorded in the Danish registers; firm accounts exist only for private-sector firms, so the public sector is omitted.
sample.unit_of_observation: firm-year (production function estimation); person-year (wage regressions); 3-digit ISCO occupation (Tables 8 and 11)
selection_rules: Keep the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in the FIRE database: Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities (more than 50% of the Danish economy and 98% of non-imputed firm-year observations)
Use all data which were not completely imputed (tax records combined with survey results)
Public-sector firms excluded: there are no accounting statistics for public sector firms
Table 1 only: restrict to ages 25-64 and years 2009-2011 for comparability with Goldin's ACS sample
Columns using the eIncome subset restrict to 2008 onward, when detailed hours are available
Occupation-level estimates (equation (6)) restrict to occupations with over 100 workers, and drop any subindustry which does not use any labor from occupation o
Table 11 keeps the occupations for which the occupation-specific productivity gap and the relevant occupation characteristic are both available (120, 115, 98, 96 and 93 occupations)
sample.n_observations: 852,729 firm-year observations in the baseline production function sample (258,978 in the 2008+ eIncome subset; 714,254 in the wage-bill sample; 641,916 in the AKM sample); 15,613,056 person-year observations in the conditional pay-gap regressions; 2,879,216 person-years in the restricted FIRE sample used in Table 1

construction_notes: Value added is revenue less the cost of intermediate inputs; value added and capital stock are constructed following the national-accounting methodology of Mortensen, Christensen, and Bagger (2010) (details in the Data Appendix).

Detailed information on the cost of intermediate goods is completely imputed for a large fraction of firms; the author uses all data which were not completely imputed, and notes the resulting measurement error is on the left-hand side.
About 9,000 firms are actually surveyed in each year; firms with more than 50 employees are surveyed annually, 20-49 employees every other year, 10-19 every fifth year, 5-9 every tenth year.

Efficiency units of labor are predicted from an earnings regression (1) run on the subsample of male workers, with a quadratic in age, a quadratic in experience, three education indicators, 225 binned-hours indicators, 3-digit ISCO occupation indicators and year fixed effects; female labor is valued with the same male coefficients.

Alternative labor measures: the firm wage bill; person fixed effects from an AKM decomposition (3)/(5); and the Griliches (1957)/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske (1999) categorical aggregator (2) with the Black-worker category dropped.
About 15% of the hours data in eIncome are imputed; IDA hours are bracketed into four bins of weekly hours (0-8, 9-17, 18-27, 27+) or monthly hours (0-38, 39-77, 78-116, 117+).

Average tenure by occupation is measured as average years of employment by men at a given firm, by 3-digit ISCO; only a top-coded measure is observed for workers who stay at the same firm for the whole window, affecting 4.7% of observations.
The flexibility index is the Goldin (2014) measure extended by Bang (2021); high numbers indicate an inflexible occupation (lawyers = 1.1).
In the occupation-level estimation of Table 10, beta_M for the category 'unknown' is restricted to be one.

claims.statement: In Danish register data for 2009-2011, the raw (unconditional) gender earnings gap in Denmark is 27.7 log points (Basic specification).

treatment.label: Female (an indicator for the worker being a woman)

register_source.value: IDA / eIncome: worker gender in the Danish registers

definition.value: An indicator equal to one if the worker is a woman, entered in a log-earnings regression alongside hours, a quadratic in age, education level dummies, year dummies and, sequentially, a quadratic in experience, occupation and industry fixed effects, and the interaction of firm and occupation fixed effects.

timing.value: fixed worker characteristic; earnings measured in the same year

outcome.label: log earnings

register_source.value: eIncome (monthly total pay) and IDA (annual payments), linked to FIRE

definition.value: log earnings of a worker in a year, from the Danish income registers (eIncome linked to IDA/FIRE); the dependent variable of the residual wage-gap regressions.

timing.value: measured contemporaneously, in the same year as the controls

units.value: log points (the coefficient on the female indicator in a log-earnings regression)

magnitude.interpretation: The author reports the gap in log points and compares it with Goldin's (2014) US estimate on the same specification ladder.

estimand.target_population: Employees in the Danish register data covered by the sample restrictions of this regression
estimand.formal_query: E[log earnings | female = 1, X] - E[log earnings | female = 0, X] for the conditioning set X of this column

population.description: Employees aged 25-64 in the restricted FIRE sample of large Danish industries, 2009-2011, chosen for comparability with Goldin's (2014) ACS sample for the US.
population.selection: Restricted FIRE sample of large industries; ages 25-64 only; the public sector is absent because firm accounts do not exist for it.

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is a cross-sectional comparison of the earnings of men and women with the same observed characteristics. Gender is not randomly assigned.

key_assumptions.assumption: Gender is not randomly assigned, so the estimated coefficient on the female indicator is a descriptive conditional gap, not the causal effect of gender; the author states that including controls in a wage regression does not isolate the causal impact of gender.

Hours worked are measured with error: hours are bracketed in IDA and salaried workers in eIncome are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime, so the residual gap may still reflect unmeasured hours differences between men and women.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author shows the measured gap falls from 16% to 10% when the better eIncome hours are used, and that bracketing alone accounts for a two percentage point increase in the pay gap.

key_assumptions.assumption: Employees aged 25-64 in the restricted FIRE sample of large industries in 2009-2011; the public sector is omitted because there are no accounting statistics for public sector firms.

implies_edges.from: employed in the sampled firms/industries

threats_discussed: Hours worked are bracketed in the IDA data, which the author shows raises the measured pay gap by about two percentage points
Unobserved differences in experience and occupational choice between men and women
Firm-level sorting of women into lower-paying firms
Omission of the public sector from the FIRE-linked sample
robustness_checks: Sequentially adding experience, occupation and industry fixed effects, and firm x occupation fixed effects (Table 2)
Comparison with Goldin's (2014) ACS estimates for the US on the same specification ladder (Table 1)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition of firm pay premiums by gender (Section 3.4.1)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured hours worked on margins the register data cannot capture
Non-wage compensation differences across firms

estimator.value: OLS

estimation.specification: Log earnings regressed on an indicator for female together with the controls and fixed effects listed; the paper prints no equation for this regression.
controls: quadratic in age

sample_n.value: 2,879,216 (restricted FIRE sample, stated in the table note)

ambiguities: Table 1 also reports four US rows taken from Goldin (2014); those are not this paper's own Danish estimates and are not extracted as claims.
The table prints the coefficient on female as a negative number; the text describes it as the size of the gap (e.g. '27.7 log points').

evidence.how: The paper prints no significance stars and no test against the relevant null. Comparing the printed point estimate -0.277 with the printed standard error 0.0011 against the null value 0.0 gives |estimate - null|/SE = 251.82, which is above the conventional 1.96 two-sided 5% critical value.

timing.value: contemporaneous firm-year t

estimand.formal_query: beta in L_jt = beta*L_F,jt + L_M,jt, the labor-preserving trade-off between men and women; under profit maximization with wages taken as given, w^f_jt / w^m_jt = beta.

population.description: Firm-year observations from the FIRE firm-accounts register linked to employee records in eIncome/IDA, restricted to the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities); private sector only.

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).

theory_referenced: Profit maximization with wages equal to marginal revenue product (the firm's first-order condition implies w^f/w^m = beta)

anchor_quote.text: Table 4 presents my baseline estimates of the relative productivity of women compared to men via the translog production function in (4). I find that one unit of female labor is equal to about 0.92 units of male labor.

claims.statement: One efficiency unit of female labor is worth 0.928 units of male labor in the translog production function (Efficiency units allow occupation to be interacted with hours).

treatment.label: female labor (female efficiency units in the firm)

register_source.value: eIncome (occupation, monthly pay and hours) and IDA (gender, children's birthdates, education, age, experience), linked to FIRE firm accounts

definition.value: Worker gender. Firm labor is aggregated as L = beta*L_F + L_M, where L_F and L_M are the sums of predicted efficiency units of the firm's female and male employees; efficiency units are predicted from earnings regression (1) estimated on male workers only, with a quadratic in age, a quadratic in experience, education indicators, binned-hours indicators, 3-digit ISCO occupation indicators and year fixed effects. beta is the number of male efficiency units one female efficiency unit replaces.

timing.value: measured in the same firm-year t as output

outcome.label: log firm value added (revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs)

register_source.value: FIRE (Regnskabsstatistikken) firm accounts: revenue and the cost of intermediate inputs; capital stock

definition.value: log firm value added, log(Y_jt - M_jt): firm revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs, constructed from the FIRE firm accounts following the national-accounting methodology of Mortensen, Christensen, and Bagger (2010); it is the dependent variable of the translog production function (4).

timing.value: contemporaneous firm-year t

units.value: beta: male efficiency units replaced by one female efficiency unit (1 = equal productivity; 0.92 = 8% less productive)

magnitude.interpretation: The same table prints relative female wages for this sample, w_f/w_m = [0.861]; the productivity gap is smaller than the pay gap.

estimand.target_population: Male and female workers in private-sector Danish firms in the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities)
estimand.formal_query: beta in L_jt = beta*L_F,jt + L_M,jt, the labor-preserving trade-off between men and women; under profit maximization with wages taken as given, w^f_jt / w^m_jt = beta.

population.description: Firm-year observations from the FIRE firm-accounts register linked to employee records in eIncome/IDA, restricted to the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities); private sector only.
population.selection: Conditioned on the firm appearing in the FIRE firm-accounts register with data that were not completely imputed, and on being in one of the six largest 2-digit industries. Public-sector firms are omitted because there are no accounting statistics for public sector firms.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation across firms and years, within 2-digit industry, in the gender composition of the workforce measured in efficiency units, related to firm value added. Gender is not randomly assigned; the author states that the gender productivity gap and the gender pay gap are fundamentally descriptive statistics.

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

implies_edges.from: unobserved firm TFP (omega_jt)
implies_edges.to: female share of firm efficiency units

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm value added is generated by a translog production function in labor and capital (equation (4)), with industry fixed effects and (in most columns) industry-specific labor and capital coefficients.

formal.as_written: log(Y_jt - M_jt) = a_jt + gamma_i + sum_{i in I} 1{j in i} ( alpha_{1,i} log(L_jt) + alpha_{2,i} log(K_jt) + alpha_{3,i} log(L_jt)^2 + alpha_{4,i} log(L_jt) log(K_jt) + alpha_{5,i} log(K_jt)^2 )

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on working in a private-sector firm with firm accounts: the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, is omitted.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5 shows women become about two percentage points less likely to work in the private sector after motherhood, and the author argues this selection out of the data is negative.

implies_edges.from: works in a private-sector firm with firm accounts

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity
Gender segregation across occupations and industries, so that a female worker at a particular firm may not be representative of female workers overall
Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)
The 2008+ eIncome subset with better measures of hours (Table 4, columns (4)-(6)) and more detailed efficiency units
CES aggregation of male and female labor instead of perfect substitutes, and CES in education with the Autor-Goldin-Katz elasticity (Table 6)
Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)
Unmeasured discrimination by the employer
The value of amenities not included in compensation, which may mean mothers are overpaid relative to productivity
Hiring and promotion-based discrimination ('mommy tracking'), which the paper says is not addressed

population.description: Firm-year observations from the FIRE firm-accounts register linked to employee records in eIncome/IDA, restricted to the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities); private sector only.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

claims.statement: Relaxing perfect substitutability between male and female labor, the relative productivity of female labor is 0.868.

treatment.label: female labor (female efficiency units in the firm)

register_source.value: eIncome (occupation, monthly pay and hours) and IDA (gender, children's birthdates, education, age, experience), linked to FIRE firm accounts

definition.value: Worker gender. Firm labor is aggregated as L = beta*L_F + L_M, where L_F and L_M are the sums of predicted efficiency units of the firm's female and male employees; efficiency units are predicted from earnings regression (1) estimated on male workers only, with a quadratic in age, a quadratic in experience, education indicators, binned-hours indicators, 3-digit ISCO occupation indicators and year fixed effects. beta is the number of male efficiency units one female efficiency unit replaces.

timing.value: measured in the same firm-year t as output

outcome.label: log firm value added (revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs)

register_source.value: FIRE (Regnskabsstatistikken) firm accounts: revenue and the cost of intermediate inputs; capital stock

definition.value: log firm value added, log(Y_jt - M_jt): firm revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs, constructed from the FIRE firm accounts following the national-accounting methodology of Mortensen, Christensen, and Bagger (2010); it is the dependent variable of the translog production function (4).

timing.value: contemporaneous firm-year t

units.value: beta in a CES aggregator of male and female efficiency units (1 = equal productivity)

magnitude.interpretation: The elasticity of substitution between male and female labor is between 5 and 10, which the author reads as suggesting perfect substitutes is not an unreasonable assumption.

estimand.target_population: Male and female workers in private-sector Danish firms in the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities)
estimand.formal_query: beta in L_jt = beta*L_F,jt + L_M,jt, the labor-preserving trade-off between men and women; under profit maximization with wages taken as given, w^f_jt / w^m_jt = beta.

population.description: Firm-year observations from the FIRE firm-accounts register linked to employee records in eIncome/IDA, restricted to the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities); private sector only.
population.selection: Conditioned on the firm appearing in the FIRE firm-accounts register with data that were not completely imputed, and on being in one of the six largest 2-digit industries. Public-sector firms are omitted because there are no accounting statistics for public sector firms.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation across firms and years, within 2-digit industry, in the gender composition of the workforce measured in efficiency units, related to firm value added. Gender is not randomly assigned; the author states that the gender productivity gap and the gender pay gap are fundamentally descriptive statistics.

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

implies_edges.from: unobserved firm TFP (omega_jt)
implies_edges.to: female share of firm efficiency units

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm value added is generated by a translog production function in labor and capital (equation (4)), with industry fixed effects and (in most columns) industry-specific labor and capital coefficients.

formal.as_written: log(Y_jt - M_jt) = a_jt + gamma_i + sum_{i in I} 1{j in i} ( alpha_{1,i} log(L_jt) + alpha_{2,i} log(K_jt) + alpha_{3,i} log(L_jt)^2 + alpha_{4,i} log(L_jt) log(K_jt) + alpha_{5,i} log(K_jt)^2 )

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on working in a private-sector firm with firm accounts: the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, is omitted.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5 shows women become about two percentage points less likely to work in the private sector after motherhood, and the author argues this selection out of the data is negative.

implies_edges.from: works in a private-sector firm with firm accounts

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity
Gender segregation across occupations and industries, so that a female worker at a particular firm may not be representative of female workers overall
Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)
The 2008+ eIncome subset with better measures of hours (Table 4, columns (4)-(6)) and more detailed efficiency units
CES aggregation of male and female labor instead of perfect substitutes, and CES in education with the Autor-Goldin-Katz elasticity (Table 6)
Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)
Unmeasured discrimination by the employer
The value of amenities not included in compensation, which may mean mothers are overpaid relative to productivity
Hiring and promotion-based discrimination ('mommy tracking'), which the paper says is not addressed

timing.value: contemporaneous firm-year t

units.value: beta: male efficiency units replaced by one female efficiency unit (1 = equal productivity; 0.92 = 8% less productive)

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

treatment.label: female labor supplied by mothers (female, children, efficiency units)

register_source.value: eIncome (occupation, monthly pay and hours) and IDA (gender, children's birthdates, education, age, experience), linked to FIRE firm accounts

definition.value: Gender crossed with parenthood: women with at least one child recorded in the register data. Firm labor treats men, women with children and women without children as perfect substitutes, L = beta_{F,c}*E_{F,c} + beta_{F,nc}*E_{F,nc} + E_M, with efficiency units predicted from the male earnings regression (1). Children are identified from the birthdates of all children in IDA.

timing.value: measured in the same firm-year t as output

outcome.label: log firm value added (revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs)

register_source.value: FIRE (Regnskabsstatistikken) firm accounts: revenue and the cost of intermediate inputs; capital stock

definition.value: log firm value added, log(Y_jt - M_jt): firm revenue minus the cost of intermediate inputs, constructed from the FIRE firm accounts following the national-accounting methodology of Mortensen, Christensen, and Bagger (2010); it is the dependent variable of the translog production function (4).

timing.value: contemporaneous firm-year t

units.value: beta: male efficiency units replaced by one efficiency unit of labor supplied by mothers (1 = equal productivity)

magnitude.interpretation: The same cell prints the relative wage of this group in brackets, [0.831]; the author notes that across industries relative wages and relative productivity line up nearly perfectly for mothers but are unrelated for non-mothers.

estimand.target_population: Male and female workers in private-sector Danish firms in the six 2-digit (NACE) industries with the largest number of firm-year observations in FIRE (Accommodation and food services, Construction, Manufacturing, Wholesale and retail trade, Other community/social/personal services, Real estate/renting/business activities)
estimand.formal_query: beta in L_jt = beta*L_F,jt + L_M,jt, the labor-preserving trade-off between men and women; under profit maximization with wages taken as given, w^f_jt / w^m_jt = beta.

population.description: Firm-year observations in the Manufacturing 2-digit industry only, from the FIRE firm-accounts register linked to eIncome/IDA.
population.selection: Conditioned on the firm appearing in the FIRE firm-accounts register with data that were not completely imputed, and on being in one of the six largest 2-digit industries. Public-sector firms are omitted because there are no accounting statistics for public sector firms.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation across firms and years, within 2-digit industry, in the gender composition of the workforce measured in efficiency units, related to firm value added. Gender is not randomly assigned; the author states that the gender productivity gap and the gender pay gap are fundamentally descriptive statistics.

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

implies_edges.from: unobserved firm TFP (omega_jt)
implies_edges.to: female share of firm efficiency units

key_assumptions.assumption: Firm value added is generated by a translog production function in labor and capital (equation (4)), with industry fixed effects and (in most columns) industry-specific labor and capital coefficients.

formal.as_written: log(Y_jt - M_jt) = a_jt + gamma_i + sum_{i in I} 1{j in i} ( alpha_{1,i} log(L_jt) + alpha_{2,i} log(K_jt) + alpha_{3,i} log(L_jt)^2 + alpha_{4,i} log(L_jt) log(K_jt) + alpha_{5,i} log(K_jt)^2 )

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on working in a private-sector firm with firm accounts: the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, is omitted.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5 shows women become about two percentage points less likely to work in the private sector after motherhood, and the author argues this selection out of the data is negative.

implies_edges.from: works in a private-sector firm with firm accounts

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity
Gender segregation across occupations and industries, so that a female worker at a particular firm may not be representative of female workers overall
Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)
The 2008+ eIncome subset with better measures of hours (Table 4, columns (4)-(6)) and more detailed efficiency units
CES aggregation of male and female labor instead of perfect substitutes, and CES in education with the Autor-Goldin-Katz elasticity (Table 6)
Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)
Unmeasured discrimination by the employer
The value of amenities not included in compensation, which may mean mothers are overpaid relative to productivity
Hiring and promotion-based discrimination ('mommy tracking'), which the paper says is not addressed

estimator.value: Translog production function regression (equation (4)); beta is the coefficient on female efficiency units inside the labor aggregator

estimation.specification: Equation (4) estimated separately within the Manufacturing industry, with men, mothers and women without children treated as perfect substitutes.
controls: log capital stock and its square
log labor and its square
log labor interacted with log capital
worker age, experience, education, 3-digit ISCO occupation and binned hours (embedded in efficiency units via equation (1))
estimation.clustering: Standard errors bootstrapped (50 samples) at the person level to account for estimation error in forming predicted efficiency units and then, for each estimate of efficiency units, cluster bootstrapped at the firm level in the production function estimation step

log firm capital stock (and its square, and its interaction with log labor)
worker age and experience (quadratics), education, 3-digit ISCO occupation, binned hours worked, year, via the efficiency-units regression (1)

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity
Gender segregation across occupations and industries, so that a female worker at a particular firm may not be representative of female workers overall
Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)

Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity
Gender segregation across occupations and industries, so that a female worker at a particular firm may not be representative of female workers overall
Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)
The 2008+ eIncome subset with better measures of hours (Table 4, columns (4)-(6)) and more detailed efficiency units
CES aggregation of male and female labor instead of perfect substitutes, and CES in education with the Autor-Goldin-Katz elasticity (Table 6)
Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)

key_assumptions.assumption: Male and female labor are perfect substitutes in production up to the scalar beta: total labor is L = beta*L_F + L_M.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 6 relaxes it with a CES aggregator and estimates an elasticity of substitution between male and female labor of between 5 and 10, which the author reads as support for perfect substitutes.

key_assumptions.assumption: A woman with the same characteristics as a man would have the same returns to those characteristics, so efficiency units predicted from the male-only earnings regression (1) measure the quality of female labor; any deviation is attributed to gender-based productivity differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5 reports alternative labor-quality measures (wage bill, AKM person effects, Griliches categorical aggregator) that do not rely on this mapping.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on 2-digit industry, capital and the observable labor quality that enters efficiency units, the gender composition of a firm's workforce is uncorrelated with the firm's unobserved total factor productivity (no sorting of women into less productive firms).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.4.1 estimates AKM firm effects separately for men and women and finds no average difference (a 0.005 log point difference); Figure 1 shows the distribution of the change in beta when an Olley-Pakes control function is added by 2-digit industry, with a large mass at 0; Table 7 adds an Olley-Pakes control and a calibrated negative-sorting term.

threats_discussed: Sorting of women (and of mothers) into firms with unobservably lower total factor productivity

Unmeasured differences in skills, in hours worked, and unmeasured discrimination by the employer
Omission of the public sector, a disproportionately female part of the Danish economy, because firm accounts do not exist for it
Endogeneity of input choice: labor and capital are chosen by firms on the basis of productivity known to them
Imputation of the cost of intermediate goods for a large fraction of firms
robustness_checks: Alternative measures of labor quality: wage bill, wage bill including non-wage benefits, AKM person fixed effects, and the Griliches/Hellerstein-Neumark-Troske categorical aggregator (Table 5)
The 2008+ eIncome subset with better measures of hours (Table 4, columns (4)-(6)) and more detailed efficiency units
CES aggregation of male and female labor instead of perfect substitutes, and CES in education with the Autor-Goldin-Katz elasticity (Table 6)
Olley-Pakes control function for unobserved TFP, overall and by 2-digit industry (Figure 1, Table 7)
A calibrated simulation imposing negative sorting of mothers into less productive firms (Table 7)
Card-Cardoso-Kline AKM decomposition to check whether women work in lower-pay firms (Section 3.4.1)
Estimation by industry (Table 9), by broad occupation (Table 10) and by 3-digit ISCO occupation (Table 8)
Restricting to the roughly 9,000 firms actually surveyed in detail about their accounts (footnote 7: beta = 0.94)
unresolved_confounders: Unmeasured differences in skills between men and women
Unmeasured differences in hours worked (salaried workers are listed as working 37 hours a week unless they clock overtime)
Unmeasured discrimination by the employer
The value of amenities not included in compensation, which may mean mothers are overpaid relative to productivity
Hiring and promotion-based discrimination ('mommy tracking'), which the paper says is not addressed
